fixes.explanation: Nope, this one's true, baker. Verse 4 says, "Wealth attracts many friends…" Solomon isn't cheering it on. He's watching how people act, and I think it stings a little. The verse sets a crowd of friends right next to a poor man who is deserted by his friend, and that contrast is the whole point.

The king isn't in this verse, baker. Verse 14 says, "Houses and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD." Notice the contrast: houses and wealth come down through inheritance, from fathers. A prudent wife is put in a different column, from the LORD. The verse doesn't spell out what makes her prudent. It only tells us where she's from.

Elders aren't in this verse, baker. Verse 14 says, "Houses and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD." Houses and wealth get passed down from fathers, but the verse points somewhere else for a prudent wife. I think that's the teaching: some things can be inherited, and this one is from the LORD.

The king isn't in this verse, baker. Verse 17 says, "Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender." A loan means you hand something over and expect it back. Here the one who is kind to the poor is the lender, and the verse says the LORD will repay. So kindness to the poor counts as a loan to the LORD, not a gift to the king.

True, baker. Verse 17 says, "Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender." The kindness is treated like a loan, and the person who showed it is the lender. The verse says the LORD will repay. I think that makes a small kindness look a lot bigger than it feels at the time.

This one's true, baker. Verse 17 says, "Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender." Solomon calls kindness to the poor a loan, which makes the kind person the lender. The One who repays is the LORD, and that's right there in the text. So "False" sells the verse short.

Strangers don't come up in this verse, baker. It says, "The desire of a man is loving devotion; better to be poor than a liar." Solomon puts being poor and being a liar side by side and says poor is better. I think his point is that honesty is worth more than a fuller wallet. The word that fits is liar.

This one is true, baker. Verse 23 says, "The fear of the LORD leads to life, that one may rest content, without visitation from harm." Solomon links the fear of the LORD to life, and to resting content without visitation from harm. It's one chain in the verse: fear of the LORD, then life, then rest. So "False" breaks a link the verse puts right in place.

That would be the opposite, baker. Verse 27 says, "If you cease to hear instruction, my son, you will stray from the words of knowledge." Learning is what hearing instruction leads to, but this verse is about the person who stops hearing. Solomon says that one will stray from the words of knowledge, which means moving away from them, not toward them. So the verse is a warning to keep listening.
